# nova-sprint roadmap

<!-- Generated from docs/roadmap.sexp by tools/roadmap. Do not edit this file: edit docs/roadmap.sexp and run `make roadmap`. -->

The plan from 2026-10-27. nova-sprint is rebuilt as a tight engine and a policy layer, one layer at a time from the bottom, each layer secured to the bar and adopted into the live sprint before the next part starts. Every release cuts nova-tools and nova-sprint together at one version. The roadmap before this plan, with every item it held, is in docs/roadmap_old.sexp; an item there comes back here only when it is part of this plan.

## The layered rewrite: an immaculate engine and Starlark policy

nova-sprint is far too large for what it is: at main 16b1c740 (2026-10-26) about 196k hand-written lines of Go, 223k of tests and 400k generated, with the CLI as heavy as the engine and steps functions of 400 to 600 lines. At heart it is a card dealer: a queue of cards with needs, dealt to workers, tracked through reads, CI and landing, refusing what breaks the rules. The rewrite splits it in two with one interface between. The engine is Go, fixed, modelled in TLA+ and locked: the store, the card machine, the steps (each one legal move with its refusals, checking a move and never choosing one) and the edges. The policy is changed during a sprint without a new binary: data tables for what is only numbers and lists, Starlark scripts for logic. The interface is the snapshot policy may see and the decisions it may ask for; the script proposes and the engine disposes. The test of which side code belongs on: if being wrong can corrupt the sprint (two writers, a lost landing, a card in two states) it is engine; if it only makes the sprint slow, costly or badly ordered it is policy. The engine is held to an immaculate bar: small, every line earning its place, no special case, every guarantee modelled and every refusal tested; whatever cannot meet that goes to Starlark or data. Each layer is secured to the bar (modelled with reversed witnesses, tested on a real store including every refusal, a second reader's probes green, used for real work, documented, then locked with Glenn) before anything above it starts. Every part is adopted at once: it lands on main, ships in the next release within a day, and runs the live sprint before the next part of its layer starts; a part not yet run in real use is not done. Until the rewrite is through, a change to nova-sprint deletes more than it adds. Source: Glenn, 2026-10-26 and 2026-10-27: "I also agree it is very large for what it actually is."; "Start with the first layer securing tonight. Work in small parts."; "once we have secured layers, actually use and adopt the fixed stuff soon, so we are not off doing large changes without actually verifying them"; "OK approved. go starlark"; "I want our part that is not starlark to be immaculate"; "We create a tight engine here now."

### Layer 1: the store

Engine. Cards, rows and the event log on nova tables; the layer to secure is the engine and tick above the generated wire code. Its parts are the layer-1 group below.

Already in the code: internal/sprint/store, about 64k lines with tests; store/engine.go 2,750 lines, store/tick.go 2,379, store/mem.go 1,573; the contract docs/layers/L1-STORE-CONTRACT.md.

Why it waits: In progress since 2026-10-26.

### Layer 2: the card machine

Engine. The states and transitions of one card (add, take, finish, read, land, hold, retire) as one module, model first, with the reference model as the oracle.

Already in the code: tla/CardMachine.tla and internal/sprint/refmodel (about 10k lines).

Why it waits: Waits for layer 1 and rocketnet M1.

### Layer 3: the steps, the engine's vocabulary

Engine. One step per legal move (deal, take, finish, read, land, hold, stop), each a pure function from snapshot and request to plan or refusal, split along the card machine's transitions; no function longer than a screen. A step checks a move and never chooses one.

Already in the code: internal/sprint/steps_*.go; steps_work.go alone is 4,322 lines with functions of 494 and 593 lines, much of it policy inside the moves.

Why it waits: Waits for layer 2 and the interface.

### Layer 4: the edges

Engine. Git and landing, CI receipts, friends' hooks and the bus: each a separate adapter with a narrow contract, faked in unit tests.

Already in the code: pkg/friend, internal/ci, cmd/nova-sprint/reads.go, cmd/nova-sprint/land.go.

Why it waits: Waits for layer 3.

### The interface: snapshot and decisions

Between engine and policy: the snapshot policy may see (a typed, versioned schema) and the decisions it may ask for, each mapping onto one step. The models take policy as any choice of these decisions, so every invariant holds for every script. Drafted as docs/layers/INTERFACE.md while layers 1 to 3 are secured, settled with Glenn before layer 3 is cut to it.

Why it waits: Drafted alongside layers 1 to 3.

### Layer 5: policy data

Policy. Numbers and lists (tiers, routes, widths, deadlines, thresholds, read mix, costs) in one versioned policy table in the store, changed by a coordinator verb that checks it and replays it against recent real snapshots before it takes effect; every decision records the version that made it; rollback is one verb.

Already in the code: Spread over nova-config rows and the set and stream set knobs.

Why it waits: Waits for the interface.

### Layer 6: policy scripts in Starlark

Policy. Deal order, when to raise a judgment, when to stop a stream, rework routing, as Starlark (go.starlark.net) functions from snapshot to decisions: deterministic, hermetic, with a step bound per tick. Scripts live in the store, versioned, set only from the coordinator seat; a new version replays against recent snapshots and is refused on any error; a failure at tick time falls back to the last good version. Policy has its own unit tests. A tracer bullet may come first: the deal order alone, behind a flag, on the live sprint.

Why it waits: Waits for layer 5.

### Layer 7: the CLI, the dashboard and replay

Thin verbs that parse, call a step and print, under 10k lines from about 115k; a policy change goes through the same checked path. Dashboard and replay are read-only views.

Already in the code: cmd/nova-sprint/verbs.go is 4,930 lines with 140 functions; internal/sprintdash, internal/sprintreplay.

Why it waits: Waits for layer 6.

## Layer 1, the store: the parts in order

The store's contract is docs/layers/L1-STORE-CONTRACT.md: what it owns, its 24 guarantees, its refusals, which model and test covers each, and the parts below in order, each landable alone. Parts 1 and 2 shipped in v1.6.26 and ran the live sprint on 2026-10-27.

### Part 1: the dead exports out of production

Five exports with no production caller deleted, three read only by tests moved into observe_test.go; the ten Mem setters stay, as tests in other packages call them.

Already in the code: Landed in #620, shipped in v1.6.26, ran the live sprint 2026-10-27.

Why it waits: Done.

### Part 2: the models cite Store.Run by its parts

DirtyTickRead, AttemptsEpochs and the COVERAGE row cite the parts of Store.Run, not line numbers; the 12 groups re-ran on a bench.

Already in the code: Landed in #622, shipped in v1.6.26.

Why it waits: Done.

### Part 3: StoreFence, the fence and commit core modelled

tla/StoreFence.tla holds G3 to G7 and G14: Acquire, the manifests, Commit, the caller-op check, Repair (the repairer sends the manifests itself; abandons past the grace, or at once on a rule refusal), writes outside the fence and Clear, with operation ids as the code builds them. It lands with its records once the two holes it found are fixed or held as named failing cases, and the COVERAGE file list names lock.go.

Already in the code: #625 (the first draft, which a cold read found unsound) is held; branch l1/store-fence-v2 at c9404753 is the revision: ten cases on hetzner2, each as declared.

Why it waits: Waits for the store-holes decisions.

### Part 4: Mem and Redis agree

Fix the two divergences (Mem ignores an unreadable timer record; Mem's commit can stop partway, recording the caller's result without emptying the fence), each with a test that runs the same call on Mem and the fake Redis client.

Why it waits: After part 3.

### Part 5: every refusal tested on Mem

The 16 refusals no test names, one small test each.

Why it waits: After part 4.

### Part 6: every refusal tested on a real store

redis_sprint_functional_test.go extended to every refusal of the contract's section 3.

Why it waits: After part 5.

### Part 7: no real time in the store's unit tests

machine_twoloops_test.go (a real sleep), tick_ask_test.go (time.Now) and waitlog_test.go (a real 30-second timeout) take a fake clock or move to the functional tier.

Why it waits: After part 6.

### Part 8: stream remove behind a store step

cmd/nova-sprint/verbs.go deletes rows of two tables outside the fence and not atomically; make it one fenced operation.

Why it waits: After part 7.

### Part 9: the teardown keys

archive, cardcheck and refusedrecord are on neither teardown list: a functional test that writes each and tears down decides whether they join machineKeys.

Why it waits: After part 8.

### Part 10: Store.Run split along its seams

The pin and caller-op check; the pre-plan enrichment handed in from above; the STOP and queue fences as a hook of layer 2; and the core read, plan, acquire, apply, release loop left in engine.go.

Why it waits: After parts 3 to 6 are green.

### Part 11: the step constructors out of the store

steps.go's 50 step constructors move to layer 3: the steps import the store, never the other way round.

Why it waits: After part 10.

## Holes the fence model found in the store

StoreFence v2 (branch l1/store-fence-v2, 2026-10-27) models operation ids as the code builds them and abandonment at once on a rule refusal. Two of its counterexamples are holes in the code, each checked against the code by hand. Each is fixed engine-side, modelled first.

### Two runs of one caller operation share an operation id

Two runs of caller operation c at one epoch both build the id c~e-1 (engine.go operation ids, schema.go OpFamily), and Release matches the fence by that id alone. When the first run's operation is abandoned at once on a rule refusal, the retry acquires the fence under the same id, and the first run's late Release(op, false) empties the retry's fence mid-operation; the retry's commit then writes nothing and reports ok. No timing assumption is needed. The fix: a per-writer nonce in the operation id, which closes it in the model (MCStoreFence passes with it; MCStoreFenceSharedOpIds is the code today).

Why it waits: Found 2026-10-27; the fix is the next engine change.

### A refusal a later write undoes

A writer delayed between Acquire and its first send can have its operation abandoned at once on a rule refusal (MEMBEREXISTS); if a later operation's plan makes that expectation hold again (deleting the member), the delayed writer's manifest applies inside the other operation's fence, and its release writes nothing and reports ok. A nonce does not close it; a fence check on manifests or a guard in the table layer would. First confirm that a real plan can undo such a refusal (unverified), then model the fix (MCStoreFenceRevivedRefusal).

Why it waits: Found 2026-10-27; one step unverified.

## Releases

Every release cuts nova-tools and nova-sprint together at one version (Glenn, 2026-10-27: "Please unify version between nova-tools and nova-sprint. This means always cut both at the same time."; "go back to releasing together so the same version is deployed across both."). One combined build: the nova-tools release carries the nova-sprint tools of the same version, and every machine runs that one version.

### v1.6.27: nova-tools and nova-sprint together again

The first release cut together since the split at v1.6.13: one combined build (the nova-tools tools and the nova-sprint tools at v1.6.27 on the four Unix platforms; nova-tools alone on windows-amd64, since nova-sprint does not build there), both tags cut together.

Already in the code: Cut 2026-10-27: nova-sprint v1.6.27 at 4172720a and nova-tools v1.6.27 at 6697d8c0, both published. Installed on the studio (all 25 tools; the sprint server, friend-sync, dashboards, hook-serve and the launchd hook clients restarted); the new server dealt a card at 14:52 and johnny finished one at 14:56. The red nightly test that held the cut was fixed in nova-tools #6093.

Why it waits: Done.

### v1.6.27 on every machine

The fleet benches still run older tools: adopt v1.6.27 on each through the fleet play (nova-sprint adopt or nova-update release adopt), Windows members taking the nova-tools tools alone, then check each member's version, its hook and one card's take, work and finish on it. The friends' own hooks running inside their sessions take v1.6.27 when those sessions next restart.

Why it waits: Next; the studio runs v1.6.27 since 2026-10-27.

### nova-sprint builds for Windows

cmd/nova-sprint/seat_environment.go uses syscall.Stat_t, so nova-sprint does not build for windows-amd64 and the Windows members carry the nova-tools tools alone. Split the file by build tag so the combined release covers every platform.

Why it waits: Small; the next release.

## Small fixes found on the way

Defects the cold reads of 2026-10-27 found in work already on main. Each is a small fix for the next release, modelled where it touches a state machine.

### log --json cuts at 20 lines by default

nova-decide reads full nova-sprint log --json exports and ignores the more field, so an export made without --max 0 is silently short. Make the export path ask for every line, or have nova-decide refuse more: true.

Why it waits: The next release.

### The friend-stage lane is not in ServerLanes.tla

The served friend stage runs on its own lane and takes the serial line twice with the line released mid-batch (serve.go); model the lane and its two-lock order in ServerLanes.tla.

Why it waits: The next release.

### Friend-stage revalidation does not compare the epoch

revalidateFriendStageSnapLocked compares kind, branch and start head but not the epoch, so a clear and re-deal during a clone can publish a JOB.md whose FINISH names the old epoch. Add the epoch to the comparison.

Why it waits: The next release.
